explanations.explanation: That's the plan, friend. The text says the spies were hoping to catch Him in His words in order to hand Him over to the governor. Everything else about them is costume: the polite faces, the sweet talk, the whole act. It's a trap wearing its Sunday best.

I see why you'd think so, but the text never says that. The spies are hoping to catch Him in His words, then hand Him over to the governor. Earlier, the scribes and chief priests were actually afraid of the people (Luke 20:19). So the crowd isn't what they're working on. His words are.

The text never mentions an address, friend. These spies aren't hunting for a place. They're hoping to catch Him in His words, and then hand Him over to the rule and authority of the governor. They brought a question, not a map.

explanations.answer: Is it lawful to pay taxes to him
explanations.explanation: That's the question: “Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” Taxes, friend. Even my mustache gets nervous at that word. And notice they only give Him two choices, yes or no.

explanations.answer: Is it lawful to bow down to him
explanations.explanation: Bowing never comes up here. The spies ask, “Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” It's a question about taxes, plain and simple. I think a question about money lands closer to home than one about bowing. Either way, taxes is what the text says.

explanations.answer: Is it lawful to fight against him
explanations.explanation: Nobody mentions fighting in this passage. The spies ask, “Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?” That's it, friend. No swords, no battle plans, just a question about taxes.

True. The text says, “But Jesus saw through their duplicity…” (Luke 20:23). Duplicity means two faces, one sweet and one sneaky. The spies practiced that smile for a while, I bet, and it didn't matter one bit.

The text says the opposite: “But Jesus saw through their duplicity…” (Luke 20:23). Duplicity means putting on one face while hiding another. The spies pretended to be sincere, and Jesus saw straight through it. Their act didn't fool Him for one second, friend.

“Caesar’s,” they answer. Jesus asked whose image and inscription were on the denarius, and the answer was right there on the coin. Think about that, friend. The spies are the ones answering, and their own answer sets up what Jesus says next.
Not quite. The spies answer, “Caesar’s.” Herod was tetrarch of Galilee (Luke 3:1), a different name altogether. The coin they were looking at carried Caesar's image and inscription.

Close to the neighborhood, but no. Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea (Luke 3:1), and he's not the name the spies give. They answer, “Caesar’s.” That's whose image and inscription were on the denarius.

explanations.answer: Give Caesar what is his and God what is His
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” He asks them to show Him a denarius, then answers them with it. It's a short answer, friend, and it doesn't leave the spies much to grab onto. I wish my answers landed like that when somebody asks me if the cookies are done.

explanations.answer: Give Caesar nothing and give God everything
explanations.explanation: That's not what He says. Jesus says, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” Caesar gets a mention, and so does God. Nothing in His answer says to give Caesar nothing.

explanations.answer: Give God first and Caesar what is left over
explanations.explanation: That's a neat order, but Jesus doesn't say it. His words are, “Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.” There's no first place, no second place and nothing about what's left over. He names both and says to give each what is theirs.
The text says the opposite, friend. “And they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people.” They came with a plan, a question and a lot of flattery. They walked away with nothing.

False, and the text is clear: “And they were unable to trap Him in His words before the people.” Then it adds that they were amazed at His answer and fell silent. They set the trap, and it never closed. I know that feeling, friend. I once built a cookie pyramid, and it also did not go as planned.
True. Luke 20:27 calls them the Sadducees, “…who say there is no resurrection…” Then they come to question Him about it. They walk in with their position already baked, friend.

The text says the opposite. The Sadducees are described as people “…who say there is no resurrection…” That's why their question is so interesting, since they're asking about something they say won't happen. They came with their minds already made up.

explanations.answer: Marry the widow and raise children for his brother
explanations.explanation: That's it. The Sadducees say Moses wrote that “…the man is to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him.” So the living brother steps in for the one who died. It's a lot to ask, friend, but that's what they quote.

explanations.answer: Look after the widow until she marries again
explanations.explanation: That's not what the Sadducees quote. They say Moses wrote that the man is “…to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him.” The man marries her himself. Looking after her until someone else comes along isn't in what they say.

explanations.answer: Give the widow his brother's land and house
explanations.explanation: Land and a house would be a nice gift, but it's not what the Sadducees quote. They say the man is “…to marry his brother’s widow and raise up offspring for him.” The focus is on marrying her and raising offspring. No property, friend.

None. The Sadducees say the first one “died childless,” and then that “…all seven died, leaving no children.” Seven brothers is a lot to keep track of, friend, so here's the easy number: zero. It's a sad story, and it sets up the question they bring to Jesus.
Not the youngest. The Sadducees say “…all seven died, leaving no children.” That includes the last brother too. Nobody in this story gets a child.

The second brother doesn't leave a child either. The Sadducees say the second and the third married the widow, and that “…in the same way all seven died, leaving no children.” All seven means all seven. The count of children stays at zero.
Wife. They ask, “So then, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? For all seven were married to her.” Seven marriages, one woman, one question. My head hurts just counting, friend.
Sister doesn't fit, friend. The Sadducees ask, “…whose wife will she be?” Their whole point is that “…all seven were married to her.” It's a question about marriage.
Servant never comes up. The Sadducees ask, “…whose wife will she be?” and then they add, “For all seven were married to her.” It's a question about marriage, friend.

The text says the opposite. Jesus says those considered worthy of the age to come and the resurrection “…will neither marry nor be given in marriage.” (Luke 20:35) He starts by saying the sons of this age marry. Then He says it works differently in the age to come.

False. Jesus says those considered worthy to share in the age to come and in the resurrection “…will neither marry nor be given in marriage.” (Luke 20:35) That's the age to come, and He sets it apart from this age. This is a hard thing the Sadducees asked, and Jesus answers it right there.

explanations.answer: Because they are like the angels
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says: “…they can no longer die, because they are like the angels.” (Luke 20:36) The reason is given right there in the verse. I'd call that a pretty big promise, friend.

explanations.answer: Because they never sinned on earth
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that. He says, “…they can no longer die, because they are like the angels.” (Luke 20:36) The reason is right there in the verse. Nothing about sinning on earth appears in His answer.

explanations.answer: Because they live far from the earth
explanations.explanation: Distance isn't what Jesus talks about. He says, “…they can no longer die, because they are like the angels.” (Luke 20:36) That's the reason He gives. No travel plans, friend.

True. Jesus says, “And since they are sons of the resurrection, they are sons of God.” (Luke 20:36) Coming from a stamper who once lived in a junk drawer, friend, that hits me right in the mustache. It's good news.

The text says the opposite. Jesus says, “And since they are sons of the resurrection, they are sons of God.” (Luke 20:36) He calls them sons of the resurrection first, and then sons of God. That's His answer to the Sadducees.

Living. Jesus says, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive.” He points to Moses, who calls the Lord “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” That's how Jesus answers the Sadducees, using Moses himself.

Nations isn't the word. Jesus says, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living…” The contrast is between the dead and the living. Jesus is using what Moses says about “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

Prophets isn't in the verse, friend. Jesus says, “He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive.” The contrast He draws is between the dead and the living. Nothing in His answer mentions prophets.

explanations.answer: They don't dare question Him any further
explanations.explanation: That's the ending: “And they did not dare to question Him any further.” (Luke 20:40) Nobody is out of questions, friend. They just don't dare to ask Him more.

explanations.answer: They bring Him an even harder riddle
explanations.explanation: No second riddle shows up here. The text says, “And they did not dare to question Him any further.” (Luke 20:40) They stop asking. The quiet is the ending.

explanations.answer: They ask Him to show them a sign
explanations.explanation: No sign is requested in this passage. It ends with, “And they did not dare to question Him any further.” (Luke 20:40) They stop asking questions. That's the whole ending, friend.
